wine.name: Riesling Clos Sainte Hune
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, as Alsace law asks of any wine labelled with one grape.
wine.sites: Clos Sainte Hune, a parcel of the Rosacker Grand Cru on the slope above Hunawihr, held by the family for more than two centuries: marly limestone over Muschelkalk and Lettenkohle bedrock.
wine.making: Fermented dry over three or four weeks in temperature controlled stainless steel, or in old casks when the year and the volume of juice call for it, with no malolactic conversion, and bottled in the spring after the harvest. The bottles then rest in the house's cellars at Ribeauvillé for some five years before release.
wine.glass: Lime peel, green apple and white peach over crushed limestone and a smoky, saline edge; bone dry, taut and long. Age brings petrol, beeswax, dried lemon and toast.
wine.ageing: Closed and severe for its first decade, it opens slowly after ten years and keeps for thirty and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, never an old one; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The parcel's name as the label has printed it since the 1919 vintage, Ste for Sainte, after the saint of Hunawihr.
The regional appellation: the label names no Grand Cru, though the parcel lies inside the Rosacker.
The grape, and the whole of the wine, as an Alsace varietal label requires.

records.table: From a family parcel inside the Rosacker Grand Cru at Hunawihr comes Trimbach's Clos Sainte Hune, a Riesling whose label names only Alsace. Bone dry and held five years before release, it is taut and stony young, so offer it with ten years behind it.
records.story: Riquewihr is where the Trimbach story starts: in 1626, by the house's own account, a Trimbach from Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines was received as a citizen of the town and took up the vine there. The family moved its house to Ribeauvillé, a few kilometres north, in 1920. Between the two towns lies Hunawihr, named, as the clos is, for Saint Hune, a noblewoman of the seventh century who, the legend goes, washed the clothes of the poor; she was made a saint in 1520. The family has held its parcel above the village for more than two centuries; the first label to bear the clos's name, of a design unchanged since, dates from the 1919 vintage. The appellation Alsace came in 1962 and the Grand Cru tier in 1975, and the hill around the clos was later classified as Grand Cru Rosacker. Trimbach chose to keep that name off the label and sell the wine as Alsace under the clos's own name, dry, with no malolactic conversion, and only after some five years in its cellars. The family bought vines on the Schlossberg in 2012, and that wine has carried the Grand Cru name since the 2014 vintage; Clos Sainte Hune never has. Its label shows plainly that a parcel's own name can say more than its appellation.

wine.name: Gewurztraminer Vendange Tardive
wine.classification: Vendanges Tardives, a legal late harvest mention of the Alsace appellation, defined in 1984
wine.grapes: Gewurztraminer alone, picked late and very ripe.
wine.sites: The house's oldest vines, in its parcels of the Sporen Grand Cru just outside Riquewihr, on clay and marl of the Lias, decalcified at the surface; the label names no cru.
wine.making: Picked by hand in a late pass at or above the legal minimum ripeness, with no sugar added, the harvest declared in advance and checked by the authorities. The juice settles for a few hours and ferments in temperature controlled casks or vats; racked once before winter, the wine clears naturally and is bottled in the spring.
wine.glass: Lychee, rose petal and candied ginger over quince paste, orange peel and acacia honey; rich and unctuous, its sweetness lifted by a faint bitter grip at the finish.
wine.ageing: Open and perfumed on release, it deepens for ten to twenty years in a good vintage, turning towards dried apricot and saffron.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour, with foie gras, Munster or a fruit tart.

label.means: Late harvest of a noble grape at a set minimum sugar, with no chaptalisation; rich, or at times nearly dry.
The grape, written in Alsace without the German umlaut; Gewürz is German for spice.
The appellation; the late harvest words are a mention added to it, never an appellation of their own.

records.table: Late picked Gewurztraminer from the house's oldest vines in the Sporen, made with no added sugar, is what Vendange Tardive means at Hugel, the family that drafted the rules made law in 1984. Pour it for its lychee, rose and ginger, rich enough to meet foie gras.
records.story: The Thirty Years War had not yet ended when a Swiss-born Hugel settled at Riquewihr in 1639, by the family's own account, and was made a freeman of the town; his descendants have made wine there ever since. Their cellar keeps a cask of 1715, the Sainte Catherine, which the house says Guinness has recognised as the oldest working cask in the world. After the hot summer of 1976, Jean Hugel (1924 to 2009), known as Johnny, is credited with first putting the words Vendange Tardive on late picked wines, words that then had no meaning in law, and he drafted rules to give them one. In 1984 French law defined both late harvest terms: the four noble grapes alone, a minimum sugar for each, the picking declared in advance and checked, and no sugar added. Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris must reach a higher minimum than Riesling and Muscat. Hugel long left its Grand Cru names off its labels, so its late harvest Gewurztraminer speaks of Riquewihr and the year, though it grows in the Sporen. When the 2021 vintage brought a compulsory sweetness mention to Alsace whites, the two late harvest terms were spared it. Every bottle is the law of 1984 at work: late picked, nothing added, its sweetness the grape's own.

wine.name: Riesling Rangen de Thann Clos Saint Urbain
wine.classification: Alsace Grand Cru, from the southernmost of the fifty-one sites
wine.sites: Clos Saint Urbain, the domaine's monopole within the Rangen above Thann, around a chapel of Saint Urbain built in the fifteenth century: volcanic greywacke and tuff on a very steep slope above the river Thur.
wine.making: Whole bunches are pressed slowly and the juice ferments with its own yeasts in old oak foudres, often for months, and it may stop before all its sugar is gone, leaving the touch of sweetness that the index on the label reports.
wine.glass: Smoke, struck flint and crushed dark rock over lime, quince and candied ginger; dense and powerful, at times with a touch of sweetness, and a long, almost salty finish.
wine.ageing: Smoky and closed for its first five to eight years, it then opens and lasts twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Grand Cru above Thann, volcanic and very steep, the southernmost in Alsace.
The domaine's monopole inside the Rangen, named for the fifteenth century chapel of Saint Urbain among its vines.

records.table: On the volcanic Rangen above Thann, the southernmost Grand Cru of Alsace, Zind-Humbrecht farms Clos Saint Urbain, and its Riesling smells of smoke and struck flint. It can keep a touch of sugar, and the domaine's own sweetness index on the label says how much.
records.story: Two families' vines became one domaine in 1959, when a Humbrecht grower of Gueberschwihr, from a family that had tended vines there since 1620 by its own account, married a daughter of the Zind family of Wintzenheim, and the domaine took both names. Far to the south, above Thann, the Rangen had almost fallen out of use: by the end of the 1960s phylloxera, two world wars and the toil of its slopes had left only a small part of the hill in vine. In 1977 the family bought Clos Saint Urbain there, named for the chapel among its vines, and replanted the neglected slope. The Rangen was classified Grand Cru in 1983, and in 1989 the founders' son became France's first Master of Wine. The domaine came to be known for very low yields, slow ferments with the grapes' own yeasts in old casks and, from 1997, biodynamic farming, certified in 2002. With so many of those ferments stopping short of dryness, it began printing its own sweetness index, from 1 to 5, on its labels, years before Alsace law made a sweetness mention compulsory with the 2021 vintage. Clos Saint Urbain puts the Rangen in one bottle: volcanic rock, a hand worked slope and a label that warns the guest how sweet the glass will be.

wine.name: Riesling Grand Cru Schlossberg Cuvée Sainte Catherine
wine.classification: Alsace Grand Cru, from the Schlossberg, the first site classified, in 1975
wine.sites: Old vines on the lower part of the Schlossberg, the steep granite hill above Kientzheim and Kaysersberg, where the wines come out fuller than higher up; the walled Clos des Capucins lies at its foot.
wine.making: A selection of old vines from the domaine's Schlossberg parcels. Pressed gently and gradually, the juice ferments slowly with its own yeasts alone in the old oak foudres of the domaine's cellar, by the domaine's own account of its method.
wine.glass: Ripe peach, lemon curd and orange zest over crushed granite and white pepper, with a hint of rose; dry, broad and rich, yet driven by firm acidity.
wine.ageing: Charming young, it gains depth for ten to fifteen years, and a strong year keeps for twenty and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant only a young bottle, and briefly; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The granite Grand Cru of Kaysersberg and Kientzheim, the first classified, in 1975.

records.table: Domaine Weinbach's Cuvée Sainte Catherine is a house name, not a site: Riesling from old vines low on the granite Schlossberg, the first Grand Cru of Alsace. It is fuller than the domaine's other Schlossberg wines, with ripe peach and lemon held by firm acidity.
records.story: The walled vineyard below the Schlossberg is recorded as early as 890, and in 1612, as the domaine tells it, Capuchin friars built their house there; the little stream that runs through it, the Weinbach, or wine stream, later gave the estate its name. The Revolution took the friars' clos and sold it as national property, and in 1898 two Faller brothers bought it and passed it on to the next generation of the family. The granite hill above became the first Grand Cru of Alsace in 1975. After the head of the family died in 1979, his widow and their two daughters carried the domaine on, and they built its name for ripe, perfumed wines called after the family rather than after sites: Cuvée Théo for the late husband, Cuvée Laurence and Cuvée Sainte Catherine, an old vine selection from the lower slope of the Schlossberg. Each cuvée is a selection of parcels within a site, fermented with its own yeasts in old foudres. The vineyards came to be farmed biodynamically, and the women of the family made the domaine a house that a guest knows by its first names. Hence the rule its labels teach, that in Alsace a cuvée may honour a person while only the cru tells you where the grapes grew.

wine.name: Altenberg de Bergheim Grand Cru
wine.appellation: Alsace Grand Cru Altenberg de Bergheim
wine.classification: Alsace Grand Cru, one of the two whose rules admit a blend of grapes
wine.grapes: A field blend of many varieties planted together in the same rows, Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer chief among them, picked and fermented as one.
wine.sites: The domaine's parcels of the Altenberg above Bergheim, a south facing slope of hard Jurassic limestone over marl, with seams of pink sandstone and iron rich clay.
wine.making: The varieties of a parcel are picked together, pressed slowly as whole bunches, for as long as twelve hours, and fermented with their own yeasts in large old foudres, where the wine is raised for about a year. It often keeps some natural sugar.
wine.glass: Candied orange, quince and dried apricot over ginger, honeycomb and a salty, chalky grip; broad and textured, often a little sweet, with a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and closed in its youth, it opens after five to eight years and lasts twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

records.table: No grape appears on Domaine Marcel Deiss's Altenberg de Bergheim, because the Grand Cru admits a field blend: several varieties grown side by side, picked and fermented together. Rich, textured and often a touch sweet, it tastes of the hill before any one grape.
records.story: The Deiss family had grown vines at Bergheim since 1744, but the domaine that carries the founder's name dates from 1947, when he came home from the Second World War and set up on his own, selling wine by grape, as Alsace did. His grandson took charge in 1973, after studying oenology, and came to argue that the grape was hiding the place: the old vineyards of Alsace, he held, had been planted with many varieties together, and the great hills were known by name long before anyone sold their wine by grape. He replanted parcels with mixed varieties, farmed them biodynamically and labelled them by site alone, at first against the rules, which asked a Grand Cru for a single noble grape. The argument won ground. In the 2000s the rules of the Altenberg de Bergheim were rewritten to admit a blend of the hill, and Kaefferkopf, admitted in 2007 as the fifty-first Grand Cru, took blends as well. When each Grand Cru became an appellation of its own in 2011, the Altenberg kept that right in its own rules. The domaine bottles the Altenberg, the Schoenenbourg and the Mambourg as field blends, each named for its hill. The Altenberg answers an old Alsace question: a Grand Cru may name its place and no grape at all.

report: Rechecked with seven searches on 12 November 2026; the domaine's own site was not reached, so every fact beyond the library rests on two secondary sources or on the domaine's sheet on a merchant's host, listed in reviews/recheck-alsace.json.

Confirmed: the founding in 1947 after the founder's return from the war, the family at Bergheim since 1744, the grandson in charge from 1973 after studying oenology (one source says 1981), and the co-planted Altenberg labelled by place.

The making and the site are now the importers' accounts: whole bunches pressed slowly for up to twelve hours, native yeasts, about a year in large old foudres; hard Jurassic limestone over marl with pink sandstone and iron rich clay.
The year the Altenberg's rules admitted the blend is 2001 by one importer and 2005 by another, so the story says the 2000s.
The founder is named only in the house's name, for want of his dates; the grandson and his son are living and are not named.
